questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the "double le" pattern tell you?
Where is the completed-action le placed, and where is the new-situation le placed?
What is this pattern sometimes called?
How is le written when it comes in the middle of a sentence?
Write the Chinese question meaning "How long have you been here?"
What are the two English glosses given for le...le?
Write the Chinese for "I have been here three days."
Give the alternative translation of Wǒ láile sāntiān le.

answers.answer_text: "I have been here three days so far."

questions_and_answers.question_text: Does the double le tell you the activity has stopped?

answers.answer_text: No — it tells you the activity has been going on and that it is still going on.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Why is le attached to the verb in láile duō jiǔ le?

answers.answer_text: Because it comes in the middle of the sentence, being followed by a duration phrase.

articles.text:
7. A: Nǐ láile duō jiǔ le?                  How long have you been here?
   B: Wǒ láile sāntiān le.                  I have been here three days.

Notes on No. 7

le...le, "up until now," "so far": The use of completed-action le after the verb and of new-situation le after the duration phrase tells you how long the activity has been going on and that it is still going on. The answer could also have been translated "I have been here three days so far." This pattern is sometimes called "double le."

Notice that when le is in the middle of a sentence (in this case, because it is followed by a duration phrase), we write it attached to the verb before it: láile duō jiǔ le
